claims.text: A machine-learning framework using multi-principal-element compositional descriptors and local-disorder features will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than rule-of-mixtures or first-principles methods.
The target materials are high-entropy alloys composed of multiple transition metals and suitable for thermal-insulation applications.
The target alloys have known composition ranges and baseline physical properties.
A supervised regression model will be trained on measured thermal conductivities from compositionally diverse high-entropy-alloy datasets.
The trained model will screen untested compositions for low predicted thermal conductivity.
Thermal-conductivity measurements will be standardized over a temperature range relevant to insulation applications, approximately 200–800 K.
The 3ω and laser-flash techniques are established methods for the proposed thermal-conductivity measurements.
Multi-principal-element alloys exhibit enhanced lattice distortion and mass disorder.
Enhanced lattice distortion and mass disorder increase phonon scattering.
Data-driven models can capture nonlinear interactions among compositional disorder, electron-phonon coupling, and phonon scattering.
Capturing these nonlinear interactions enables more robust predictions than first-principles calculations or simple mixing rules.
The proposed approach will reduce average phonon-transport prediction error by at least 15% relative to conventional predictive methods.
Rule-of-mixtures and standard DFT-based models are currently typical baselines for approximating high-entropy-alloy thermal conductivity.
The model will be most reliable for metallic, stable solid-solution alloys whose relevant compositional space is represented in the training data.
Predictions will be less reliable for extrapolated chemistries absent from the training data.
Large-scale, high-quality experimental thermal-conductivity datasets for high-entropy alloys are limited.
New alloys predicted to have low phonon thermal conductivity can be synthesized and benchmarked by laser-flash measurements from 300–800 K.
SEM, XRD, and TEM will be used to determine whether benchmark specimens have single-phase or dual-phase microstructures.
Prediction deviations greater than 15% for multiple new compositions would refute the claimed ML advantage.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome defines success as at least a 15% reduction in average error relative to baseline methods, whereas the falsification rule uses greater than 15% absolute prediction deviations in an undefined number of individual cases. These are different metrics, and the latter does not establish whether the ML model outperforms the baselines.
